Sauvage by Dior is a Aromatic Fougere fragrance for men. Sauvage was launched in 2015. The nose behind this fragrance is François Demachy. Top notes are Calabrian bergamot and Pepper; middle notes are Sichuan Pepper, Lavender, Pink Pepper, Vetiver, Patchouli, Geranium and elemi; base notes are Ambroxan, Cedar and Labdanum.

Dior launches its new fragrance Sauvage, with the name originating from the fragrance Eau Sauvage from 1966, although the two don’t belong to the same collection. Sauvage is inspired by wild, open spaces; blue sky that covers rocky landscapes, hot under the desert sun.

Dior in-house perfumer, François Demachy, signed this creation. The fragrance is announced as radically fresh, raw and noble at the same time. The composition is reportedly prevalent with carefully selected natural ingredients. Fresh top notes of Calabria bergamot encounter ambroxan, obtained from precious ambergris, and its woody trail.

Dior Sauvage comes out in September 2015, advertised by actor Johnny Depp. It is available as 60 and 100 ml Eau de Toilette.

Dior Sauvage Eau de Toilette opens with a bright burst of fresh citrus framed by a noticeable peppery edge. Clean aromatics support the citrus without becoming overtly herbal, while a crisp, almost metallic quality gives the fragrance its signature identity. The opening feels airy and light yet projects with surprising strength, delivering a sharp but refined freshness that immediately stands out.

After the first hour, the sharper edges soften as the fragrance settles into a woody ambroxan core. A crisp, dry wood is rounded out by a diffusive, slightly sweet ambroxan accord, while the peppery citrus remains present as an accent along with lingering clean aromatics. The combination feels surprisingly substantial while maintaining an airy, lightweight character.

By the drydown, the citrus has fully blended into the peppery woody ambroxan structure. The ambroxan becomes the defining feature, creating a smooth, diffusive woody profile that stays powerful without becoming cloying. Just enough sweetness runs through the base to keep the woods from feeling sterile, while the pepper continues to add subtle definition to the composition.

Overall, although undeniably synthetic, there is a reason Sauvage EDT has become one of the most popular men’s fragrances available. It is crisp, clean, masculine, and exceptionally versatile. If I could only own one fragrance to cover virtually every situation, this would absolutely be in consideration.

Score: 8.5/10
FragranceSpiceTeam 08/02/26 21:54

Dior Sauvage Eau de Toilette

Some fragrances become popular because of marketing. Others become popular because they simply work. To me, Sauvage falls somewhere in the middle, it had a huge marketing push, but after wearing it in different situations, I understand why it continues to have such a large following.

The opening is bright and energetic with a noticeable burst of bergamot that immediately feels clean and modern. Within the first half hour, the peppery character starts to emerge, adding just enough spice without making the fragrance feel heavy. As it settles, the woody and slightly musky base becomes more apparent, giving it a smooth finish that stays remarkably consistent.

What I enjoy most is how effortless it is to wear. It doesn't ask much from the wearer. Whether I'm heading to work, meeting friends for dinner, or attending a casual event, it rarely feels out of place. It's one of those fragrances I reach for when I don't want to overthink my choice.

Performance has always been reliable on my skin. I generally notice moderate projection during the first couple of hours before it becomes more subtle, while the scent itself lasts well into the evening. It's noticeable without being overwhelming if applied with a light hand.

Of course, its popularity is also its biggest weakness. Because so many people wear Sauvage or fragrances inspired by it, it doesn't have the element of surprise anymore. If your goal is to smell completely unique, there are plenty of more distinctive options available. But popularity doesn't automatically make something undeserving of praise.

After spending time with many designer fragrances over the years, I still appreciate Sauvage for what it is: a dependable, versatile fragrance that consistently delivers a clean, confident impression without trying too hard. It may not be the most adventurous scent in my collection, but it's one I continue to enjoy reaching for.

(4.5/5)

i keep smelling sauvage at the store, trying to find something to say about it, or form some kind of opinion. i went multiple times, hoping i can change my mind about it and see what everyone else sees in it. i like dior's other frags, and usually i'm a man of many words. i like reading the arguments y'all have with each other in the reviews. so, today's the day i finally add my contribution.

all i can really say is that it smells like my uncle's deodorant from 2010. it's giving freshly shower gel'd businessman who uses a lot of aftershave to compensate for his halitosis. or sweaty old guy with no swag, trying hard to smell good and cover up his bo with whatever product the drug store spoon-fed him on their front-and-center display at the time. it's forgettable, and it's hard to want to keep my nose in it long enough to come up with a more vivid description than that.

many women will say it's a douchebag scent that their ex wore, and the men on here make a great point: well, you slept with your ex for a reason. you must have found the scent attractive on him at some point. but as someone who doesn't sleep with men, or hang around them at all, and is thus not an expert on the male sex, i say this is a generic male fragrance for a man whose only personality trait is being male and *possibly* having above-average hygiene practices. the bar is low for men, and, in any case, these habits are futile in the face of their alarming meat consumption habits, which have an unfortunate - yet easily preventable and well deserved - influence on their body's odour.

this might be a good time to mention that the only men i ever get close enough to to be able to smell them are my uncles when i'm forced into hugging them at christmas dinner. generally speaking, if i'm close enough to smell a man, i'm closer than i want to be. so, by nature of having never smelled a man consensually, i tend to associate ultra-generic ultra-masculine scents with stinky old guys and feelings of discomfort.

all that is to say, for better or for worse, when you choose to wear a fragrance with a generic profile, you're bound to remind people of someone else. this isn't just a dig at dior sauvage in particular; it's an acknowledgement that i've smelled this same scent profile before sauvage was released. i smelled it in shower gels, deodorants, aftershaves.

and don't get me wrong, there's nothing wrong with generic! i am by no means the type of person who thinks that only the most unique and niche fragrances are good or interesting. my take on sauvage is that it just smells like shower gel and deodorant. my personal approach to perfume is that it should smell like more than just your average soap or hygiene product -- it's meant to add something to other peoples' olfactory experience of your body. it should tell people about you. if you wear vanilla, you might be a sensual gourmand. if you wear patchouli, you might be a hippie.

all sauvage seems to say about the man wearing it is "okay, so this man smells like shower products, which means he may or may not have washed his ass this morning." boring! i want a scent to give me a little bit of information about the person wearing it. when you're choosing a perfume you need to ask yourself "who, or what, do i want to remind people of?" personally, i don't get all that excited when i'm reminded of a man getting out of the shower.

Dior Sauvage Eau de Toilette is one of the most popular men's fragrances ever released, but its popularity is also its biggest weakness. It opens with a strong burst of bergamot and pepper, creating a fresh, spicy, and very recognizable scent. The ambroxan-heavy dry down gives it a clean, woody, and masculine style that is easy to enjoy.

Performance is solid, with good longevity and strong projection, but the fragrance itself can feel a little too safe and predictable. The biggest problem is that Sauvage has become extremely overused. Because so many people wear it, it has lost much of its originality and can give the impression of smelling like everyone else.

Although it has good quality and a pleasant scent, the price can feel harder to justify when there are many alternatives that offer a similar fresh and masculine style. Overall, Dior Sauvage is a well-made fragrance, but its lack of uniqueness and massive popularity make it less exciting for people who want something different. 7.5/10.

This is a bergamot and pepper dream. I'm a woman. The modern industry tells me that I should just stick to my usual female lane with rose, vanilla, sweet berries, dainty-but-exquisite white florals and white musk. So why am I experimenting with men's fragrances now?

Bergamot and pepper. That's why. Bergamot is one of my favorite notes to cut through high summer heat, humidity, and odor, and unfortunately many brands are diluting or even removing their bergamot with cheaper, short lasting citruses. These citruses smell wonderful in the opening, but then dies down quickly in less than 1 hour.

Without the strong presence of bergamot, cedar, patchouli or pepper notes to carry citrus through, it just dies. This reduction of bergamot is especially true for women's summer fragrances recently, where citruses don't last long anymore and women today anyways are now gravitating more towards sweeter and inoffensive fragrances (I am also guilty of this).

But I remember the old days where women weren't afraid of bold, bergamot forward, strong woodsy and peppery fragrances that would easily last 8-10 hours. But that has become more of a memory of the past. The 80s are gone, and they took the body with it. Hence, I've decided to venture into male fragrance territory for the modern day.

Sauvage defies the awful modern trend of skimping out on body and longevity, and brings bergamot, pepper and "woodsy" notes back to the fore front where it belongs and it remains, for more than 6 hours. I sprayed 2 sprays of Sauvage EDT 2 days ago on a test strip and it is still there today. It still shares the same core Eau Sauvage DNA, but without venturing too deep into the "1960s-babershop-aftershave" territory. The ambroxan is ok, it does smell quite synthetic in this at first, but then quiets down a bit.

After 3-4 hours, the florals really open up and smelt absolutely amazing. For this reason, I might just end up buying a bottle for myself when I have to do outdoor work in the summer.

Dior Sauvage doesn’t enter a room so much as it breaches it like an ill-planned firewall hack. It's a crypto startup kicking down the door of a WeWork conference room it didn’t book.

The opening hits you in the face with that pepper/Ambroxan nut-blast, the kind that feels less like a fragrance and more like a motivational speech delivered through a spit soaked megaphone!

This is the scent of a man who doesn’t just have the Dunning–Kruger effect, he lists it on his LinkedIn profile under “Core Competencies" like it was a badge of honor and wonders why he never gets call backs. He gets endorsed by colleagues with names like Brayden, Chase, and Zane; each with the same shit-eating grin and Patagonia vest like it was a uniform. Lord, and the endless, mindless, insufferable droning about their passive income streams and NFT portfolios...

It's no wonder why homicide rates are spiking!

Sauvage is the fragrance of a guy who treats overconfidence like a certification he earned in a paid weekend seminar. He’s not embarrassed by it, oh no, he’s proud. He’s out here adding "looksmaxxing” to his résumé and wondering why HR departments ghost him!

He describes himself as equal parts "disruptor", "visionary", and "pioneer" to anyone in a 10 foot radius.

Unironically.

Sauvage guy thinks he's a “serial entrepreneur” and networks at trade shows hoping to ground-floor some new grift like it's really the gamechanger the cold pitch claimed it was.

Get in, get off, and get out!

He abandons the start-up faster than his mom left his dad for the tennis coach. Or was is pilates instructor? Was that the same guy? Who can remember!

This is a guy that says “I don’t follow trends” while wearing the most popular men’s fragrance on Earth! Yeah, bruh, you're making your own way!

Sauvage is the scent of a man who thinks he’s the main character in a documentary about alpha hustle culture that no one is filming. He has a favorite Joe Rogan podcast episode and quotes it like scripture from the pulpit of excess.

This guy thinks sleeping only two hours a night is a mad flex!

And let's not ignore the elephant in the room any longer!

Let’s not pretend that Jeremy Fragrance is not this scent’s spirit animal.

And not in the cute and quirky way.

Not a Capybarra or Red Panda type of spirit animal.

Nooooooo.

This is an unholy abomination in a white suit sort of critter!

Two sprays of Sauvage and somewhere, a ring light flickers to life, a white marble floor materializes, and a man begins doing push‑ups while shouting “POWER!” into the void.

Sauvage doesn’t just channel Jeremy, it summons him like an Ambroxan‑soaked poltergeist. Like blooky freakin' Mary herself in the mirror!

If this fragrance had a shrine, it would be built from empty tester bottles, rambling motivational quotes written on fragrance strips, and creepy AF monologues about the thing your mom said would make you go blind!

You don’t smell Sauvage. You receive it like an unwanted push notification that you cant unsubscribe from! This is the scent of unearned confidence and repressed sexuality.

But does it work?

Sure.

In the same way a hammer works.

The same way broad spectrum antibiotics work.

In the most unsubtle, emotionally unavailable way imaginable.

Sauvage doesn’t whisper.

It doesn’t hint.

It doesn’t seduce.

It declares itself, plants a flag, and thanks you for coming to its TED Talk. It is THE MOST overconfident molocule soup on the market but sometimes you want a scent that kicks the door open, throat punches the air around you and announces your presence like a carnival barker trying to con you outta your last fiver for three chances to knock over a stack of milk bottles!

Sauvage is not nuanced.

It is not refined.

It is not soft or reflective.

But it is effective.

And honestly, that's why it's iconic.

So yes, Sauvage works.

But at what cost.

I only began getting into fragrances somewhat more seriously a few years ago, and along and along I'm trying to pick up some iconic scents for my collection. I have no preconceived notions (positive or negative) about Sauvage, having only ever smelled it in magazine advertisement scent strips. Having finally gotten it and worn it a few times, it's definitely a strong like but not a love.

This is indeed extremely mass appealing, and I can see why it sells so well. This is an all purpose, all season, all around easy reach that couldn't be more versatile. It's the kind of smell I can't imagine anyone disliking for the scent itself, though I get "toxic ex" associations that might be an issue for some. This one goes on fresh and spicy thanks to the citrus and pepper in the opening, then settles into a very ambroxan-heavy accord that's still a little spicy, woody, and fresh thanks to the prominent lavender - a nice likeable blue shower gel scent. The performance is very good, with ample sillage that's noticeable without choking out a room. For a long time I was that guy that owned 1 or maybe 2 bottles of cologne, and for old me this would have been the perfect choice thanks to it's good performance, versatility, and super pleasant scent.

But the flip side of Sauvage for me now is that it isn't particularly interesting. What it offers in mass appeal it kind of lacks in personality. I already owned Versace Dylan Blue when I got this, for example, and they're definitely of the same vein but I like Dylan Blue better thanks to it's somewhat darker more earthy dry down that gives it more character and a slightly less generic freshie feel.

Ultimately Sauvage is a very solid scent and I'm glad to have it. Is it my favorite scent I own? No, I have a bunch I like better. But it's pretty foolproof if you just want to smell good.

#100 of My Fragrance Journey - Dior Sauvage EDT: The one everyone knows. The one that still works.

The club dissolves into light and movement behind me - bodies, bass, heat folding into each other. But the terrace holds a different rhythm. Cooler. Slower. Air that feels filtered.
He's already there when I step out. Leaning against the stone, athletic silhouette cut sharp against the city lights. Still. Grounded. The kind of presence that doesn't ask for attention but takes it anyway.

And before I properly see him - there it is.
Clean, sharp, unmistakable. A line cut through warm night air.

I almost smile to myself. Of course it is.

Sauvage. The one everyone knows. The one people roll their eyes at, then recognise on instinct before they've finished the sentence. Overworn, over-discussed, impossible to ignore. For most people, it feels like a shortcut - something chosen because it works, not because it says anything.

I should dismiss it. But I don't.
Because distance is one thing. Proximity is another.

I move closer, slow enough to feel the shift. Bergamot sharpens as I enter his space - bright, almost metallic, like cold light hitting skin. Precise. Engineered. Clean to the point of abstraction. Then the warmth underneath starts to rise. Ambroxan - dry, woody, faintly smoky - pulls everything down into the body. It doesn't bloom dramatically or unfold in layers. It just locks in, responding to heat, to movement, to breath.

I thought I knew this scent, I think. Half to him, half to myself.

And standing there, I realise - I was wrong about it.

Because here it isn't the same scent I've passed a hundred times on the street. It's closer. More contained. The projection that felt loud from a distance now feels like a boundary - something you step into, not something that chases you. The brightness softens. The mineral edge warms. It becomes tactile.
There's a moment where the space between us narrows without either of us really deciding it. The scent shifts - not compositionally, but physically. Skin, heat, salt in the air. The kind of detail you don't analyse. You just register.

"You smell like everyone," I say quietly. Testing the line as much as the moment.

A pause. Not defensive. Then a faint smile.

"Yet you're still here."

It lands. Because that's the contradiction - it's everywhere, it's familiar, and still, right now, it works. Not because it's unique. Because it's effective.

It doesn't evolve much, this one. No dramatic transitions, no unexpected turns. In another context, that could feel flat. Predictable. But here it reads differently. Consistent. Controlled. Assured. The ambroxan hums close to the skin, almost weightless but persistent. Citrus softened into clean mineral brightness, sitting just above it. Nothing loud. Nothing pushing. Just present.
There's a risk, though. More sprays, more heat, less restraint - and it tips. Becomes sharp, overbearing, too much of itself. It doesn't have the complexity to recover once it crosses that line. But he hasn't crossed it. It's measured. And that restraint is what makes it compelling.

I've stopped thinking about notes. About reputation. About whether I'm supposed to like it.

What stays is simpler than that - the effect, the presence, the way it holds a moment together without trying to dominate it.
It's easy to dismiss something this popular. Easier still to forget why it became that way in the first place. But standing there, close enough to feel warmth through cool air, it doesn't feel like a cliché.
It feels like a constant.

Reliable. Familiar. And in the right moment - unexpectedly hard to walk away from.

Vibe: Cool air, warm skin, light cutting through shadow.
Performance: Strong opening, steady intimate radius. Respect the two-spray rule.
Fit: For someone who understands that effectiveness isn't the same as mediocrity - and wears it as they mean it.

So tell me - if something this familiar can still feel this magnetic in the right moment… is it really overrated, or are we just wearing it wrong?

More scent stories and visuals on Instagram - @lavendercloudsjd

Dior Sauvage EDT: The Reigning King of Blue Fragrances
I’ve used both the EDT and the EDP versions, and in my experience, the EDT is surprisingly more radiant and longer-lasting. It provides the true, authentic "Sauvage experience." People complain that "everyone smells like this" or associate it with "ex-boyfriends," but honestly, I couldn't care less—it’s a fantastic scent.

The Success Story
The Profile: When you think of "Blue Fragrances," this is one of the first two names that come to mind. It’s a complete success story with its fresh opening, peppery kick, aromatic heart, and woody touch.

The Impact: It has dominated the market since the day it was released. It’s the king of the room, not just for me, but for anyone who values a great blue fragrance.

My Journey
Loyalty: I’ve already finished a 60 ml EDT and a 100 ml EDP. Right now, I only have a 3 ml decant left just to sniff it once in a while, but I’m still obsessed. I feel like I need a 200 ml bottle to spend more good days with this loyal friend.

The "Everyone Wears It" Myth: While it was true 5 years ago that everyone was wearing it, I feel like people have moved on to other trends. But its true, loyal friends never left. It’s a timeless classic that still holds its ground.

CaptainMorganInDubai 03/18/26 23:03

Sauvage is like an old friend. I rarely reach for it these days but will never get rid of it and when it runs out I will buy another bottle. It gets an outing every few months and I still get a lot of enjoyment from wearing Sauvage. I've been wearing it since about 2016. Back in the day it was THE fragrance for guys and had an allure that you rarely see matched by anything these days. It took the blue trend fragrance was experiencing and took it in a spicer, edgier and more complicated direction. Sauvage, along with Bleu de Chanel, pretty much signalled the end of the Aquatic epoch for mainstream fragrance and can legitimately claim to be a cultural phenomenon in its own right, going above "mere" perfumery. Along with Baccarat 540, it heralded the beginning of the "Ambroxin Era" and nothing was ever quite the same again for any of us after that, was it?

So, ten years later, although Sauvage's star is unarguably on the wane, it does still wear very well and is still a legitimately great choice. It has aged better than I think a lot of people thought it would. It has certainly aged better than I have in the last ten years. It is linear but does last incredibly long for an EDT concentration.

We know the fragrance profile intimately by now and so it serves little purpose to go back through the notes and so on, but for me, the star of the show here and what makes Sauvage still wearable and still enjoyable even after all this time, is the pepper and the patchouli. It's blue Jim, but not as we know it. Believe it or not, I've actually never got my nose on the Elixir concentration of Sauvage as there is a part of me that thinks perfection should be left alone and that some things should be allowed to age gracefully. Sauvage has always felt just right for me and I cannot for the life of me see how a flanker concentration could or would improve this.

I rarely wear it now because it isn't interesting really and I've got over a hundred bottles of fragrances so its utility is always going to be limited to times when I want to feel retrospective. The traumatic first half of the last ten years were the worst of my life and there is a lot about that period that I do not ever wish to reach for or be reminded of, which I guess is another reason why. But as I said earlier, I will always have a place in my collection for Sauvage. It is the fragrance equivalent of holding onto old photographs or having that iTunes playlist from way back in the day. I still have a little bottle of CKOne for the same reason. Not to wear (I haven't for many, many years now) but to smell and be reminded of simpler but no less intense times in a world very much different and somehow more innocent than the one we live in now.

Three Word Summary: Never Been Rumbled

Scent - 8/10
Sillage - 8/10
Drydown - 6/10
Bottle/packaging - 8/10
Performance - 8/10

OK, so after reading all the shameless scathing thrown @ Dior's latest offering, I had to make a visit to my local stockist to sample what all the fuss was(n't) about.
I did the obligatory card-test first which came out as quite a strong, heavy, in-your-face blast of pepper with a hefty dose of aldehydes to boot. I then walked around the store before returning, to offer my neck and wrists a spray. I left the store and went about my business of doing some shopping.

Two hours later, the smell remained heavy on me with very good projection.

Three hours later, still no signs of letting go, this fragrance lost none of the original smell and followed me around like a stalker. Each time I turned my head, I could smell it wafting by.

Some time later on my way home as I was stood waiting for the train doors to open, the lady aside me asked: "Is it you who smells nice?" I beckoned her towards my neck to sniff. Her reply: "Yes, it's you, that's beautiful, what is it?".
An hour later buying a drink in a bar, the barman said: "You smell fresh, what are you wearing?"; before I had the chance to reply, another guy standing next to me said: "I wanted to ask the same question but was too shy".
Not one but three compliments on Sauvage within as many hours. That's most definitely a first for me. I've never been complimented more than once in a week let alone a day regarding any fragrance I'm wearing.

So, although my conclusion leaves me to say that this is by no means the best Dior fragrance I have had the pleasure to wear, I don't find it offensive in the slightest. Six hours later it's still smelling pretty strong on me, and, with (three) random strangers seemingly smitten by it, I think it will become a great seller for Dior.

Most Popular Negative Reviews

Buysblind 09/09/15 19:42

Mediocre in every sense of the word. Sauvage opens with an abrasive, chemical interpretation of bergamot that's sweet and mildly pleasant. It transitions after about 10 or 15 minutes into a peppery dryer-sheet musk that is completely flat and linear and feels even more synthetic than the opening. I guess that's the ambroxan with some pepper added to it. Projection is solid and the longevity is around 6 to 8 hours.

I disagree with anyone suggesting that Sauvage is of a better quality than the average designer fragrance on the market, at least as far as the ones in Sephora or Macy's are concerned. It's not. It smells cheaply made and totally insubstantial save for whatever overdose of synthetic fixatives keep it alive. In comparison to Bleu de Chanel, Sauvage is vastly inferior. At least Bleu has some dimension and structure. It has development and solid, robust ingredients. Sauvage is absolutely anemic aside from its caustic, searing chemical edge which seems to provide its only strength. The only positive thing I have to say about it is that the smell itself is not bad--it's not unpleasant as a scent. But what's that really saying? Scent is subjective in that regard, so really anything can be "nice" or pleasant. Cleaning products are pleasant too. So are Glade Plug-Ins and those little trees people hang from their rearview mirror. Fabuloso smells great. And that's more or less what Sauvage has successfully replicated--your basic air freshener--vaguely representing all things common in men's cologne over the last 10 years. I've worn Sauvage 7 times, searching for any redeeming qualities it might possess and other than its inoffensiveness, and the fact that I kind of like the way ambroxan smells, I have found none. What's crazy to me is a lot of the people complaining over and over again about "another generic woody-amber" somehow give Sauvage a pass. Really?

I'm not a fragrance snob or niche elitist or whatever other accusatory labels are getting thrown around to try and invalidate contrary opinions. My favorite release of the year was probably CK Reveal Men. Yet again and again I hear the same old argument, "...but this fragrance is made for the average guy, it's not for the perfumistas and enthusiasts." Well, no shit. And the average guy deserves better than this hollow, chemical dreck that wears as if it should cost $20 instead of $90, and can't hold a candle to its competition. Compliments? Who cares. Wear anything that leaves a solid trail and doesn't smell like you stepped out of a time warp or a horse stable and you WILL receive compliments. So you might as well pick up something decent while you're at it. Not this crap. Save your money.

Thumbs down.

alfarom 09/09/15 23:21

I don't know where to start with Sauvage.

For unknown reasons, I really wanted to like it. There's something about most Dior's mainstream masculines that's never *too banal* or *too cheap* and, on top of that, the association between the words Dior and Sauvage must have played some mental tricks on me and made me think about Roudnitska's classic Eau Sauvage. Ok, we all know this is not an Eau Sauvage flanker and as a new, massively advertised, delivery from Dior, I thought I couldn't have skipped it.

For starters, this is not as bad as I expected. It's not even as bad as a rushed test might lead to think….but it's bad anyway in the end.

I won't go through a proper note breakdown because there's really not much to mention here. The opening it's the most generic peppery-citrus combo you could expect from a whatever modern woody-citrus fragrance. Slightly aromatic, zingy and metallic.The first hour in, I was really this close to dismiss it but then a smooth mineral amber base (ambroxan) broke in together with vetiver and things slightly changed. The fragrance plays in the same league as other *depersonalizing*, post-disinfectant fragrances such as Bleu de Chanel, Guerlain's L'Homme Ideal and before these, D&G Light Blue Pour Homme and L'Eau D'Issey but it takes the distance from the aforementioned perfumes by skipping that certain synth-y stickiness and / or loud volume that made all of them completely annoying to me. The Dior has a certain *raison d'être* provided by an elegant restraint and a class that is completely missing in most similar fragrances available on the market. It wears smooth and velvety with nice dark-ish facets in the base. It's extremely simple but, at least, they got right one of the two accords from which it is composed.

Do I like it? Let's put it this way: It doesn't completely suck. In the end, while I surely believe Sauvage is by far the best fragrance in this post Bleu De Chanel-phase, I still wonder if we really needed a post Bleu De Chanel phase. It feels deprived of any emotional aspect but not in a creative kind of way. It's unemotional without that certain sparkle that makes the difference between the words *aseptic* and *aloof*. It feels devoided. It's carb free, gluten free, peanut free, allergens free…it's too politically correct. Ok, it's well done but for me it's not enough and, in the end, I guess it's just another fragrance for people who actually don't like fragrances.

Last but not least, I'm not the biggest fan of the Dior Homme saga but compared to this, they're completely on another level. Like completely.

Rating: 5.5-6/10

Chiru 05/27/17 14:54

Hm... not really feeling this one guys. A frustrating fragrance in that it smells very synthetic, quite cosmetic and mall-like, and given the hype I was expecting a lot more. A very boring fragrance for the man with a perfect smile. It smells "perfect" but not in a good way. This is very much a modern male fragrance for modern males in the work setting, with no differentiating characteristics. Very machine-like and fake. It's hard to explain. I hope at least someone gets this reference... I know it's stupid, but it's pretty damn accurate:

Remember that Spongebob episode where squidward wishes spongebob wasn't so goofy, and was more of a man's man agreeable neighbour? And spongebob becomes all rounded instead of square, is shiny and boring, but pleasant and agreeable, and also like every other typical guy? He just repeats "Hi, how are ya?" and seems fake? That's who I picture wearing this fragrance. Shallow, agreeable, boring yes-man guys in a suit at the office that smile at you and wave when you park your car up your driveway. Not that there's anything inherently wrong about being friendly, but you know what I mean, right? About as multifaceted as a piece of paper and about as deep as a yogurt lid.

It's just a generic, soapy department store kinda fragrance. Extremely safe, powdery, flowery, peppery and bright. I don't get the hype on this one. And I'm pretty open minded. I'm no snob who won't touch designer mainstream perfumes just because I think I'm some enlightened fellow who only sniffs interesting scents for interesting people. It just really is a boring scent, plain and simple. I know my review sounds bad, but it's not a -bad- scent per se. It's just... lacking anything to make it stand out. I'd pay maybe $40-50 for this scent. Maybe? But the asking price for this scent is absolutely insane for what it brings to the table. I have to echo what others are saying. It smells quite a bit like Bleu De Chanel, mixed with some peppery flowers and soapy powder. Perhaps people only like it because women seem to like it on men. It does have that fresh out of shower smell afterall. Thing is, every guy and their grandad wears this stuff, so for a perfume that everybody wears, it loses even more points towards purchasing it for me. How ironic that every guy wears a fragrance that just screams "every guy" in the first place. To each their own.

I'm glad I tried this first and didn't spend the asking price for this perfume. A disappointment. Gosh, it really does just smell like hotel soap, lol. Really, this stuff smells like if you got a bar of cheap Irish Spring soap and sprayed a bit of Bleu De Chanel on it. I mean I like it, please don't get me wrong, it's a very nice scent, and it does have good longevity, but at this price? And this boring? Nah. Want a typical soapy clean scent? Mugler Cologne is a lot cheaper to find and smells pretty decent. Want a subtle flowery work scent? Try Prada L'Homme which is incredible. Honestly there's just so many better options as far as soapy clean scents go that don't cost over $100 and have you smelling like every other guy. That's the main issue here. Sauvage isn't bad, it's just not good enough. Try before you buy. All scents are subjective. You may love this. I'll repeat myself here, I would absolutely buy this scent at a heavily discounted price. The drydown is pretty good, better than the opening for damn sure, but not great. If this was like $50 or lower, I'd absolutely get it. But no way in hell for the asking price right now.

And another thing! How odd they called this "Sauvage". There's nothing "sauvage" about this in any stretch of the imagination. See that picture of Johhny Depp in the pictures section for this fragrance? Even he's making a "the fuck is this shit? sauvage? are you serious?" kinda face as he stares at the big white lettering of "Sauvage".

Scent: 6/10, good drydown though.

Personal Appreciation: 6/10
